stories.title: Should Kids Get a Break From Social Media?
stories.headline_kid: Some countries are stopping teenagers from using social media apps — and Singapore is watching closely to decide what to do here.
summary: In Australia, teenagers under 16 are not allowed to have social media accounts. But many teens have found clever ways around the rule, like using fake birthdays or special apps that hide where they are. This means the ban isn't working as well as grown-ups hoped.

Malaysia tried a different approach — checking people's age before they can sign up. But this has worried some parents, because companies now need to collect more personal information, like ID numbers, just to prove someone's age.

Singapore doesn't have a full ban yet. Instead, our government is studying what worked and what didn't in other countries, so it can come up with its own plan — sometimes called a 'playbook' — that fits Singapore families best.

This matters because social media affects how much time kids spend on screens, who they talk to online, and even how they feel about themselves. Grown-ups everywhere are trying to find the right balance between keeping kids safe and letting them enjoy technology.

stories.title: Singapore's Next Big Land Trick: More Reclaimed Islands!
stories.headline_kid: Singapore is planning to create even more land by reclaiming it from the sea — here's how it's done.
summary: Singapore is a small country, so for many years it has made itself bigger by 'reclaiming' land from the sea. Think of it like building an enormous sandcastle — engineers add sand, rock and soil into the sea until new land appears above the water.

New plans could join several western islands, like Pulau Bukom, into one large island. There's also the ongoing Long Island project along the east coast, which could create new land in front of East Coast Park.

Reclamation methods have changed over time. In the past, huge amounts of sand were used, but engineers are now trying gentler, more environmentally-friendly ways to build land, especially with rising sea levels caused by climate change in mind.
This new land could one day be used for homes, factories, parks, or even to protect Singapore's coastline from flooding as the sea level rises.

lenses.world: Singapore is seen as a world leader in smart and careful land reclamation techniques.

stories.title: Why Singapore Airlines Is Sticking With Its Indian Partner
stories.headline_kid: Singapore Airlines owns a big slice of Air India, which has been losing money — so should SIA quit or stay?
summary: A few years ago, Singapore Airlines (SIA) bought part-ownership, called a 'stake', in Air India. Owning a stake is a bit like owning a slice of a pizza — you don't own the whole company, but you get a share of the profits (or losses).
Air India has been losing a lot of money while trying to improve its planes, service and reputation. This has made some people wonder if SIA made a mistake and should sell its share and walk away.

But experts say leaving now might mean SIA misses out on something bigger later. India has one of the fastest-growing numbers of air travellers in the world, and staying invested could help SIA earn a lot in the future once Air India improves.
This matters to Singapore because SIA is our national airline and an important part of our economy. Decisions like this affect jobs, flight options, and how strong SIA remains in the years ahead.

stories.title: Nepal Builds a Smarter Alarm System After Deadly Flood
stories.headline_kid: After a huge flood swept through Nepal's mountains, the country is now installing sensors and cameras to warn people of danger earlier next time.
summary: Last week, a massive collapse of rock and ice near the Nepal-Tibet border caused a terrible flood that swept away villages and buried hydropower tunnels where workers were working. Sadly, many people lost their lives, and Singapore even sent a search-and-rescue team to help.

Now, rescuers are still digging through the tunnels, hoping to find survivors. One official said he was 'very confident there is life in there', showing hope that some trapped workers may still be found alive.

At the same time, Nepal is planning something new — building an early-warning system using sensors, cameras and satellite equipment along its border with China. This system works a bit like a smoke alarm for mountains, detecting danger signs like moving rocks or rising water before disaster strikes.

Scientists warn that the ground in the area is still unstable after the huge collapse, which means more landslides could happen. The new warning system aims to give people precious extra minutes to escape to safety next time.

stories.title: Driverless Taxis Hit the Streets of London!
stories.headline_kid: Uber and a tech company called Wayve just launched London's very first taxis that drive themselves — no human driver needed!
summary: A 'robotaxi' is a taxi that drives itself using cameras, sensors and a computer brain, without a human driver behind the wheel. Uber has teamed up with an artificial intelligence (AI) company called Wayve to bring these self-driving cars to the streets of London for the first time.
The cars use AI, similar to how your phone's map app guesses the best route, but much smarter — it can 'see' pedestrians, traffic lights and other cars, and decide how to drive safely all by itself.
This is a big moment for driverless technology in the United Kingdom, and more cities around the world are watching closely to see if it works well and keeps people safe.

Singapore has also been testing self-driving vehicles for several years, including shuttle buses in places like one-north and Sentosa. London's robotaxi launch shows how fast this technology is developing, and it's possible Singapore could see more autonomous vehicles on our roads in the future too.

lenses.me: Imagine hopping into a taxi and there's no driver — just you, the car, and a computer doing the driving!
lenses.family: Your family might discuss whether they would trust a car without a human driver.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could chat about which cool tech inventions you'd like to try first.
lenses.nation: Singapore's own self-driving vehicle trials could speed up as this technology matures elsewhere.
